common_consequences.note: Adversaries could execute system commands, typically by changing the SQL statement to redirect output to a file that can then be executed.
Since SQL databases generally hold sensitive data, loss of confidentiality is a frequent problem with SQL injection vulnerabilities.

demonstrative_examples.text:
The following code dynamically constructs and executes a SQL query that searches for items matching a specified name.

Example of the weakness (C#):
```
	string query = "SELECT * FROM items WHERE owner = '" + userName + "' AND itemname = '" + ItemName.Text + "'";
```

mock_response.description: The product constructs all or part of an SQL command using externally-influenced input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could modify the intended SQL command when it is sent to a downstream component. Without sufficient removal or quoting of SQL syntax in user-controllable inputs, the generated SQL query can cause those inputs to be interpreted as SQL instead of ordinary user data.

detection_methods.description: This weakness can often be detected using automated static analysis tools. Many modern tools use data flow analysis or constraint-based techniques to minimize the number of false positives.
detection_methods.effectiveness_notes: This is not a perfect solution, since 100% accuracy and coverage are not feasible.

detection_methods.description: This weakness can be detected using dynamic tools and techniques that interact with the software using large test suites with many diverse inputs, such as fuzz testing (fuzzing), robustness testing, and fault injection.

mapping.comments: Carefully read both the name and description to ensure that this mapping is an appropriate fit. Do not try to 'force' a mapping to a lower-level Base/Variant simply to comply with this preferred level of abstraction.
mapping.rationale: This CWE entry is at the Base level of abstraction, which is a preferred level of abstraction for mapping to the root causes of vulnerabilities.

modes_of_introduction.note: This weakness typically appears in data-rich applications that save user inputs in a database.

mock_response.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')

notes.note: SQL injection can be resultant from special character mismanagement, MAID, or denylist/allowlist problems. It can be primary to authentication errors.

observed_examples.description: SQL injection in AI chatbot via a conversation message
SQL injection in e-mail agent through SQLite integration

potential_mitigations.description: Use a vetted library or framework that does not allow this weakness to occur or provides constructs that make this weakness easier to avoid [REF-1482].

If available, use structured mechanisms that automatically enforce the separation between data and code. These mechanisms may be able to provide the relevant quoting, encoding, and validation automatically, instead of relying on the developer to provide this capability at every point where output is generated.

description: Look up software and hardware weaknesses in MITRE's Common Weakness Enumeration, the catalogue that security scanners, CVE records and coding standards use to name what went wrong (CWE-79 is cross-site scripting, CWE-89 SQL injection). Turn ids from a scan or a vulnerability report into names, search weaknesses by words or by the CVEs they cite, and read any weakness in full: its consequences, how to prevent and detect it, the platforms it affects, real examples and related attack patterns. Get the Top 25 and OWASP Top Ten lists, browse categories and views, and walk the hierarchy up and down to roll findings up into broader classes. Every action reads: nothing here changes anything. No account or API key required.
